title: Staged prefill smoothing with latency-tail control
creator: Ava Chen
description: Problem: We observe elevated P99 and P999 latency spikes when large prefill batches coincide with long decode requests. Current prefill/decode splitpoint logic is binary and causes either starvation of low-latency traffic or throughput loss when we favour fairness. Goal: Design and implement a staged prefill->decode smoothing policy that dynamically chooses a splitpoint and smoothing window to trade off tail latency vs aggregate throughput while maintaining proportional fairness across customer tiers. The policy must be kernel-aware (use attention cost and kernel selection hints) and compatible with existing hedging/fallback logic.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New scheduler reduces P99 latency by >=15% for latency-sensitive routes under mixed load compared to baseline. 2) Throughput drop (tokens/sec) <=7% on best-effort routes. 3) No customer-facing errors introduced during canary. 4) Observability: per-route latency histograms, fairness quantiles, and splitpoint heatmaps available in Console.
design_decisions: - Use a two-stage smoothing window: micro-window (5-50ms) for opportunistic fastpath, macro-window (50-250ms) for fairness smoothing. - Compute per-request weight from route priority + estimated attention cost (kernel hint) to decide proportional allocation in each window. - Use quantile-based admission controller: maintain moving estimates of 90/95/99 quantiles for each route; if route's tail exceeds threshold, give it reserved micro-slices. - Prefer kernel-friendly packing: when kernel selector indicates long-attn cost, bias assignments to avoid fragmenting large KV caches. - Backoff: if smoothing causes queueing beyond deadline, fall back to strict latency-first policy for affected routes.
tradeoffs: - Aggressive smoothing improves throughput but can increase short-term latency; we limit this via micro-window caps. - Kernel awareness reduces inefficient context switches at cost of extra estimation overhead. - Quantile allocation requires additional state (memory/CPU) for histograms; acceptable at cluster-level one per host.
implementation_steps: 1. Add moving quantile tracker to request router (C++ runtime).
2. Implement smoothing allocator that splits each scheduling epoch into micro/macro slices.
3. Integrate attention-cost hint from kernel selector into allocator decision path.
4. Expose config flags and per-route parameters in Console (rolling knobs).
5. Add instrumented metrics (per-route P50/P95/P99, slice utilization, fairness score).
6. Unit tests for allocator invariants and integration tests with end-to-end workload harness.
7. Canary on dedicated pool alpha-1, monitor dashboards, iterate, then gradual rollout.
test_plan: Microbench: synthetic mix of short chat (prefill small, decode short) and long-compute requests to validate P99 improvement.
End-to-end: run customer-like traces from telemetry for 24h comparing baseline vs smoothing policy.
Chaos: inject kernel slowdown and measure fallback correctness.
Regression: ensure hedged requests and canary rollouts still behave as expected.
Load test: validate throughput under 2x peak load and confirm resource usage within limits.
metrics: Tokens/sec per host and per route
Fairness index (Wasserstein distance across route latency distributions)
Fallback invocation rate and hedged request rate
rollout_plan: Feature flag gated by cluster: runtime.smoothing.enabled
Canary group: dedicated pool alpha-1 (10% of traffic) for 48 hours
If metrics stable, expand to 50% then full rollout over 7 days
Immediate rollback if P99 increases >10% for latency-tier routes or errors increase >0.5%
